Pele Yoetz 328:3: And there is already a story told about a great wealthy man who was a great philanthropist, and an emissary came to him from the Land of Israel, may it be rebuilt and reestablished speedily in our days, Amen. And the wealthy man asked him how much was needed for the trouble of the Land of Israel to save them from their distress, and the emissary answered him, by way of parable, that a hundred thousand lions were needed [i.e., a great sum], and immediately he pledged to give him the mentioned sum and that he should return, and the emissary rejoiced greatly. And it came to pass that a great ship of his was almost lost at sea, and the wealthy man returned home downcast and grim. And the emissary, seeing his face, thought that he had retracted the gift he had pledged in the goodness of his heart while in his cups, and he began to engage him in conversation, telling him that the law is that one who pledges a great sum while drunk with wine may retract it. And the wealthy man answered him: “Heaven forbid that I retract the pledge, for I pledged it with a whole heart; I am only sad because the Name hates me and has paid me my reward immediately in this world, since my ship arrived [safely].” Then the emissary answered him: “Do not fear, your reward is very great for the World to Come. This is only the fruit of your deeds that you eat now, so that you can perform more commandments and good deeds like these.” It turns out that the perfect man ought to flee from good fortune, but when it is the Name's will, His ways are such that goodness and kindness pursue him.
Pele Yoetz 328:4: And likewise the verse that is written (Hosea 6:3), “Let us know, let us pursue to know the Lord,” means: even if a person encounters many obstacles in the service of the blessed Name, and especially regarding intention and cleaving, when thought flees from him and he cannot direct his mind, to the point that it seems to him as though the Holy One, blessed be He, flees from him and does not desire him — even so, let him not despair, but rather press forward and persist until mercy is shown to him from Heaven. And this is what they said, “Let us know, let us pursue to know the Lord.” And this follows the way the commentator explained the statement of our sages, of blessed memory (Pesachim 86b): “Whatever the host tells you to do, do, except ‘leave.’” This means: whatever the Host — that is, the Holy One, blessed be He — tells you to do, do, except “leave” — that even if the Holy One, blessed be He, were to say about you as He said about Elisha ben Abuyah, “Acher” (Chagigah 15a), “Return, wayward children, except for Acher” — press forward and enter, for that is His true desire, and in the end the Name shall help him.
Pele Yoetz 328:5: And it is fitting for a person to be among the pursued rather than among the pursuers, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Bava Kamma 93a): “Among birds, none is as pursued as turtledoves and young pigeons; therefore Scripture qualified them for sacrifice.” And they said in the Midrash on the verse (Ecclesiastes 3:15), “And God seeks the pursued” — even when a righteous man pursues a wicked man, and how much more so when a wicked man pursues a righteous man (Kohelet Rabbah, ch. 3, verse 15). Over this let the heart of those who sit on seats of judgment tremble, for sometimes they must discipline the wicked and pursue them to utter destruction, and a scale and balances of justice, in measure and weight, are needed to strike him only to the extent of his wickedness, no more, and let all his deeds be specifically for the sake of Heaven — perhaps there is hope.
Pele Yoetz 329:1: Ritzah (Running) — It is written (Psalms 119:32), “I shall run in the way of Your commandments.” And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 6b): a person should always run to perform a commandment, even on Shabbat. And they said in the holy Zohar that one who runs to perform a commandment, correspondingly above, the defending angels run and hasten ahead of the prosecuting angels. And regarding this it is said (Esther 3:15), “The couriers went out in haste by the king's command, and the city of Shushan rejoiced and was glad.” Correspondingly, one who runs to commit a transgression, the prosecuting angels hasten — “the couriers went out in haste, and the city of Shushan was confounded.” And we have likewise learned (Avot 4:2): “Run to fulfill even a minor commandment,” and we have likewise learned (ibid. 5:20): “Be swift as an eagle and run as a deer to do the will of your Father in Heaven.”
Pele Yoetz 329:2: However, the matter of running requires a measure, so that he not be called, by that very name, a “foolish pious man,” but rather should take large strides quickly, in a dignified manner befitting his honor. And this is the trait of a good man: in all his walking, even if he has no business at all, he should walk as one who has business, for one who walks slowly, heel by toe, is among the haughty of spirit. But when going to perform a commandment, he should hasten more, like one who is swift in his work to find desirable things. And when leaving the synagogue, even if he has great haste elsewhere to go to, let him walk slowly at the start of his departure, so as not to indicate that it [prayer] was a burden upon him. And running indicates love, as it is written (Song of Songs 1:4), “Draw me, we shall run after you.”
Pele Yoetz 330:1: Ribbit (Interest) — The severity involved is known: one who lends at interest transgresses five negative commandments, and his possessions collapse, and he goes down and does not rise, and he has no portion in the God of Israel (Bava Metzia 71a, 75b). And the last matter is grave: that he shall not rise at the resurrection of the dead, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Pirkei D'Rabbi Eliezer, ch. 33), that among those bones that Ezekiel revived, one remained that did not come to life, because he had lent at interest. And through our sins, this is common among many of the common people, who lend at interest because they do not know its severity. And also because the sages permitted it through a document of partnership [heter iska], they think this and that are the same, and everything has become treated as permitted to them. And there are several detailed laws regarding the laws of interest that people are not expert in, and simple folk have transgressed and been punished, and especially regarding the matter of bills and exchange transactions, many stumbling blocks have multiplied — there is outright interest and there is dust of interest [indirect forms]. May the Good Name grant atonement for this.
Pele Yoetz 330:2: And this is a consequence of the fact that, through our sins, Israel has become greatly impoverished — “the Lord is righteous, and we have transgressed and rebelled.” And whoever has fear of the Name touch his heart, if he knows he has in his possession money from interest, let him hasten to return it and not let injustice dwell in his tent, before he loses permitted money together with forbidden money. And whoever fears the Name and is concerned for his money should go to a sage and inquire to know all the laws of interest thoroughly, so as not to stumble in the sin of interest, Heaven forbid, and let him write down those laws he was not expert in, so that they be a reminder before his eyes. And let the man tremble and shrink from letting interest touch his money more than he would tremble at letting pork, forbidden fat, or blood touch his food, for in truth it is indeed more severe. For one who eats pork, forbidden fat, blood, and the like transgresses only one negative commandment, while in interest he transgresses five negative commandments. Except that I have already said that there are minor transgressions that, by chance, people are exceedingly careful about, and if wicked men were to emerge who transgress them, the whole city would be astonished at them for having departed from Jewish practice; and there are more severe transgressions that people are not careful about and have come to be treated as permitted, such as the sin of interest, slander, vain oaths, taking the Name in vain, and many other such evils, with neglect of Torah outweighing them all — let one who guards his soul guard against them all.
Pele Yoetz 331:1: Rosh Hashanah — Rosh Hashanah is the great Day of Judgment, on which “a king by justice establishes the land” (Proverbs 29:4), and all who come into the world pass before Him like sheep through a narrow gate, and regarding it is said, “concerning the countries, it shall be said,” etc., “and creatures shall be recorded,” etc., as we say in the Musaf of Rosh Hashanah. And even one who has not set his heart to fear the awesome and fearsome Name on the other days — who does not fear on this day? As it is stated in Scripture (Amos 3:6), “If a shofar is sounded in a city, shall the people not tremble?” And the kabbalists wrote that since the whole Torah is comprised of fear and love — fear regarding negative commandments, love regarding positive commandments — and man, being turbid matter, dust from the earth, is like one whose eyes are closed, sitting in a dark house where the world is dark before him, and he needs both to open his eyes and to be brought a candle so that he can see lights, for one alone does not suffice. However, when a candle is brought to him, even if his eyes are closed, he senses somewhat the candle's light, and if he opens his eyes a little he sees a little light, and according to the degree he opens his eyes, so shall he see a greater light from the great candle, a bright light. So it is with man: because the eyes of his intellect are shut from seeing intellectual matters and from striving toward this, and also because he dwells in this world, a lowly and dark world, therefore “the fool walks in darkness” (Ecclesiastes 2:14), his eyes closed to seeing, his heart lacking the intellect for how to fear and love the honored and awesome Name, and he does not feel fear and love at all, and cannot direct his mind, since he does not know the nature of love and fear except superficially, not seeing whom he must fear and whom he must love, and is not aroused to this. What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do, wishing to grant merit to Israel, His treasured people? He gave them the appointed times of the Lord, holy convocations, through which the Holy One, blessed be He, causes a flow of holiness to descend upon them and shines His light — on Rosh Hashanah and the Days of Awe, He shines the light of dread and fear.
Pele Yoetz 331:2: And this is the reason there is no person among Israel who does not feel fear and dread, each according to his own aspect and according to the preparation he made beforehand, and according to the opening of his eyes. There is one who fears with the fear of punishment and the terrors of death, and there is one who fears with the fear of majesty, and there is one whose fear is small, and there is one whose fear is great, and there is one whose fear rises higher and higher still, level upon level. And according to the flow and illumination he receives on Rosh Hashanah, so it extends over him and its impression remains for the entire year.
Pele Yoetz 331:3: And likewise on Shabbatot the light of delight shines, which is love, and every person feels delight — there is physical delight and there is spiritual delight — according to his preparation and according to the opening of his eyes, and from it is drawn forth, for all the days of the week, love of the Name and delight in the Name. And on the festivals and appointed times the light of joy shines, and every person of Israel feels joy — there is physical joy and there is the joy of a commandment, spiritual joy, subtle beyond subtlety, according to his preparation and according to the opening of his eyes, and from it is drawn that Israel rejoices in its Maker throughout the year, and this is the secret of the verse (Proverbs 16:15), “In the light of the king's face is life.” Behold, therefore, let a man gather strength on Rosh Hashanah to have his heart full of fear, trembling and quaking, from dread of the Name and the majesty of His glory. And although we have said that this depends on a person's preparations, in any case, since the gates of fear are open, when a person arouses himself he shall find help corresponding to him, and find the means of his redemption, and his soul shall live for the entire year, provided he not let his mind wander — for if throughout the entire day he is only occupied with deepening and persisting in his thought to fear the honored and awesome Name with the fear of majesty, because He is great and ruling, the root and source of all worlds, and all that stands is considered as nothing before Him.
Pele Yoetz 331:4: And the commandment of the day is to be greatly aroused with thoughts of repentance, and especially at the time of the shofar blasts, for then the King sits on the throne of judgment, and even the angels on high are seized with trembling. And it is fitting that in every congregation of Israel, the elder among them stand before the ark before the shofar blasts and speak to them words of admonition, written or oral, and cry out in a loud voice like a shofar, to inform the many what is being done on this day, how great is the power of repentance, and the like, according to his eloquence, so that they remember and repent. And after the sermon let him recite the Kaddish, and let the people respond with intention and with all their strength, for this is exceedingly beneficial for the atonement of sins, and the hour requires it. And afterward let them begin the order “At the time the gates of favor,” etc., with great humility, for humility is a great principle for atonement and for the acceptance of prayers.
Pele Yoetz 331:5: (And it grieves me that on this day everyone wants to display the pleasantness of his voice — this one jumps from one corner and raises his voice for “Who dwells [in the covenant]...” and another jumps from another corner for “He said to Abraham...” And likewise during the Amidah, who and who will display his voice to sing loudly for “I shall hope,” “And we shall remember,” and likewise on Yom Kippur. What Divine service is there in this, and what connection to the sake of Heaven does this have? This is nothing but the counsel of the evil inclination, showing off the pleasantness of his voice when the hour does not call for it, for they said in the Midrash (Rosh Hashanah 32b) that the ministering angels asked before the Holy One, blessed be He, why Israel does not recite Hallel on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and He said to them: “The books of the living and the books of the dead are open before Me, and shall they recite Hallel?” Derive from this an a fortiori argument for this matter, for display and showing off of voices is not good on these days; rather let them pray with great intention, with much humility, with a weeping voice, with pleasant speech, with clear diction letter by letter, word by word, with exceeding precision, as is fitting to do, and let them not turn to arrogance to say, “Understand my meditation,” for festivals and appointed times are one matter, and the Days of Judgment are another.)
Pele Yoetz 331:6: And in order to arouse myself and my contemporaries, I wished to copy the holy words of the divine kabbalist, our teacher Rabbi Shalom Sharabi Mizrahi, of blessed memory, brought in his holy book Nehar Shalom, of what he used to say at the time of the shofar blasts, and how good it is to expound them publicly, for his words are the words of the living God, and they are like burning coals — words that come from the heart and enter the heart, for when a person gives his spirit to them, they pierce the heart to its innermost chamber. And these are his words: it is known to my teacher, according to the plain reason for the commandment of the shofar, that it is to awaken sleeping hearts, as Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote (Laws of Repentance, ch. 3, para. 4): although the blowing of the shofar on Rosh Hashanah is a decree of Scripture, it contains a hint, as if to say: awake, you sleepers, from your sleep, and you who slumber, arise from your slumber, and examine your deeds, and return in repentance, and remember your Creator — those who forget the truth amid the vanities of the time and spend their whole year in vanity and emptiness that neither profit nor save. Look to your souls and improve your ways and your deeds; let each one abandon his evil way and his thought that is not good. And let him regret his neglect of Torah and his paucity of commandments and good deeds, and what he did that was not good — and not only regarding the deeds of the past year alone, but regarding the deeds of all the days of his life, and even regarding all his past reincarnations — for all this shall God bring into judgment.
Pele Yoetz 331:7: And now, “the shofar is blown in the city, and the people do not tremble” — “let us search and examine our ways” (Lamentations 3:40), for through our sins our mother has been sent away these many, many years (and the righteous man has been lost to the Matron [the Divine Presence]). And therefore let all the direction of our faces in our prayer be with complete intention to redeem the Divine Presence and the sparks of holiness from exile, and to break open her prison house, as is written in the Tikkunim on the verse (Exodus 2:12), “And he turned this way and that”: “Is there anyone who will awaken in repentance to break open her prison house, to say to the prisoners, ‘Go forth’ (Isaiah 49:9)? Is there anyone who will call to her in repentance, that the Holy One, blessed be He, return the Divine Presence to Himself?” But all of them cry out in their prayers on the day of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur like dogs: “Give us sustenance, forgiveness and atonement, inscribe us for life” — and they are brazen-faced, etc., and there is no one who calls to her in repentance, that the Holy One, blessed be He, return the Divine Presence to Himself. And let every man who fears the word of the Name have his heart tremble within him from dread of the Name and the majesty of His glory, and let him take to heart that today his judgment is brought before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, who judges all the earth, regarding his body, his children, and his money, and He knows all of a man's deeds, his thoughts and his schemes and all the secrets of the heart, and He needs neither witnesses nor evidence before Him, for He is the judgment, He is the witness, and He is the litigant. And fear and dread should come upon him, saying: “What shall I do when God rises, and when He visits, what shall I answer Him?” And let him examine his deeds, and in a brief moment his eyes shall see to find his sin, a thousand and ten thousand against him from his right, and he has nearly transgressed several negative commandments, and especially those that depend on the heart, such as (Leviticus 19:17), “You shall not hate your brother in your heart”; (ibid. 18), “You shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge”; “You shall not harden [your heart] nor shut your hand” (Deuteronomy 15:7) — and the positive commandments, (ibid. 10:12), “to fear the Lord, to love Him, to walk in His ways,” and the commandment of “And you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18), which is a great principle in the Torah, and it is this very thing that destroyed our house, and we have still not been purified of the plague of leprosy — the sin of baseless hatred, and slander, which is worse than idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed, and vain oaths, and taking the Name in vain, which is like a vain oath, whether in the holy tongue or in the languages of the gentiles, and robbery, deceit, falsehood, and injustice, and neglect of prayers, blessings, and commandments, and similar minor and severe transgressions — our hand has found them abundantly. Over this let all who mourn mourn: was man created for this, to transgress his Maker's will, Heaven forbid, or perhaps was life and peace given from Heaven to waste time on vanity and emptiness, when a person is judged for every single moment and is asked how he spent every moment, as it is written (Job 7:19), “You do not let me alone even to swallow my spittle”?
Pele Yoetz 331:8: And the sin of neglecting Torah outweighs them all. “For what did the land perish? Because they abandoned My Torah” (Jeremiah 9:11; see Bava Metzia 25a; Midrash Eichah Rabbah, introduction, letter 2), and the beginning of a person's judgment is regarding words of Torah (Shabbat 31a), and every hour and every moment that one does not engage in Torah is called a deficiency that cannot be counted, and whoever does not engage in Torah is called “rebuked,” for he has despised the word of the Lord (Numbers 15:31), and every day a heavenly voice goes forth and says (Avot 6:2): “Woe to creatures for the insult to the Torah,” and even one who sits idle is called a scoffer, one of the four categories [that do not receive the Divine Presence], and how much more so one who speaks idle talk, which is a positive prohibition (Yoma 19b): “You have wearied the Lord with your words,” and it is written (Amos 4:13), “And tells man what is his speech” — even matters of no substance are written down and read before Him on the Day of Judgment (Chagigah 5b) — woe to that shame, woe to that disgrace, and how much more so one who stumbles in the sin of the four categories that blemish all four worlds, Atzilut, Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah, namely: scoffers, flatterers, liars, and tale-bearers of slander. And every single sin is a painful thorn to the Divine Presence, and strengthens her prison house and adds pain to her pains, and what does the tongue say? “My head is heavy for Me,” etc., “This recompense I hoped for, woe, for my children have left me,” the young woman cried out, “the Lord has given me into hands I cannot withstand.” And engagement in Torah, which rectifies for the sake of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence, must be for its own sake, without any ulterior motive, as is written in the Tikkunim: a voice goes forth every night and says, “What shall I proclaim?” (Isaiah 40:6) — “Go and tell them to occupy themselves with Torah, to raise up the Divine Presence and unite her with her husband, but there is no one who awakens her toward her husband, no one leads her and no one holds her hand, for through our sins our mother has been sent away,” as written above.
Pele Yoetz 331:9: And now is a time of favor; let us be strong and strengthen ourselves to subdue our hearts and return in complete repentance, for the gates of repentance are open today, and this is what we seek on this very day, for the entire essential rectification of the shofar above depends on repentance, and a great necessity is the arousal of the heart in repentance on this day, for the sound of the shofar does not act above unless the sound rises with the arousal of the heart in repentance, and if not, it is like a musician merely playing music. And even if a person has in his hand a sin among those sins that delay repentance — such as having been a cause of leading his fellow to sin during an arousal of repentance — on this day it causes the gates of repentance to be opened for him, for the gates of repentance are open, and a small arousal of repentance today is worth as much as great effort at another time.
Pele Yoetz 331:10: And therefore now is the time to be gracious to her, a time of favor, to regret with complete regret all our folly and all our sins, general and specific, and let each of us accept upon himself to repent of some sin in his hand, and let none of us fall short of repenting some sin, whether minor or severe, for through this he merits to be a righteous penitent and tips the scale for himself and for the entire world toward merit. And the early authorities wrote that whoever does not repent during those days before Rosh Hashanah, and is inscribed and sealed on Rosh Hashanah among the wicked, if he contemplates repentance on that very day in the congregation, the evil of his verdict shall be torn up and he shall be inscribed in the Book of Life, since the gates of repentance are open, as it is written (Isaiah 55:6), “Seek the Lord while He may be found.” And let all the direction of a person's repentance and prayers be for the exile of the Divine Presence and for the destruction of our holy and glorious House, for every generation in whose days the Holy Temple was not built, it is as though it were destroyed in its days (Yerushalmi Yoma 1:1; Midrash Tehillim 137:10), and especially in this generation, when all the appointed times have passed and the matter depends only on repentance — “Come, let us return.” This is the summary of the words of the holy master, of blessed memory.
Pele Yoetz 331:11: Your own eyes see that it is a great principle to accept upon oneself to repent of some sin in one's hand, but no one takes it to heart, for they worry they cannot withstand it. But an obligation rests upon us to accept it without a vow and to stand on guard with all our strength, and the Lord God shall help us, for one who comes to purify himself is assisted from Heaven (Shabbat 104a). And happy are the Israelites, most of whom, during these two days, do not cease their mouths from study, and recite Psalms, and some recite them twice, so that it turns out they recite three hundred psalms, corresponding to the numerical value of “village” [a mnemonic]. But it is known, the statement of our sages, of blessed memory (Tur, Orach Chaim, sec. 1): better a little with intention than much without intention. And how good it is, when reciting the psalms, to always intend the meaning of the words, and especially on these days, most of which are supplications and awesome prayers said with divine inspiration, and certainly bear fruit above. And if he does not know the meaning of the words, in any case let him read letter by letter, word by word, for if he reads quickly, “who can discern errors?” (Psalms 19:13) — and let him intend that they contain deep secrets, and that he intends according to the mind of King David, peace be upon him. And wherever “enemies,” “haters,” “adversaries,” and the like are mentioned, let him intend the prosecuting angels, for they are the true enemies, enemies of the Name and enemies of our souls. And wherever “trouble,” “distress,” and the like are mentioned, let him intend the trouble of the soul, for “trouble” is its name. And when reciting Psalms with humility from the depth of the heart, with intention directed toward the desires of Heaven — and these are ancient matters, words of the living God spoken from the mouth of the holy divine King David, may his merit protect us — they shall certainly bear fruit, and he shall find the means of his redemption, and be inscribed in the Book of Good Life, which is the life of the soul, as I have written above under the entry Selichot — see there.
Pele Yoetz 331:12: And wherever one requests “life” in prayer, besides that there are deep secrets referring to the Divine Presence and the sparks of holiness, let him also intend the life of the soul, that he live feeling fear and love of the Name all his days. And let him also intend the life of the body, that he wishes to live in order to serve his Creator and complete the rectification of his soul, spirit, and higher soul, so that there be no grief or anger to the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence on his account, and with this intention he should ask greatly for the life of the body, for one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world is better than all the life of the World to Come (Avot 4:17), and this shall be his intention when he says, “Remember us for life,” etc., “for Your sake, O living God.” Examine, deepen, and elaborate on this, for this is the whole of man.
Pele Yoetz 332:1: Rabbim (The Many) — Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Torat Kohanim, Leviticus 26:8): the many who perform commandments are not comparable to the few who perform commandments, for it is more exalted, whether because “the Mighty God does not despise” (Job 8:20) — and even if there are sinners among them, and even if some perform the commandment without proper devotion and reverence and not as it should be, it ascends above with favor and satisfaction before our Father in Heaven — or because “in the multitude of people is the king's glory” (Proverbs 14:28), and how many good qualities attach to communal Torah study and communal prayer and every commandment performed communally. Behold, therefore, it is fitting for every person to associate with those who fear the Name and esteem His Name, and fulfill the statement of King David, peace be upon him, who said (Psalms 119:63), “I am a companion to all who fear You,” provided that no mishap result from that association and it not become a commandment fulfilled through transgression — such as if it leads to dispute or forbidden speech and the like, in which case he should hold aloof; but if he can bring merit to the many so that they perform a commandment properly, how good and pleasant that is.
Pele Yoetz 332:2: And just as a commandment is exalted and gains added strength when performed communally, correspondingly, a transgression committed communally is a doubled and multiplied evil, and adds strength to the Sitra Achra. And it is a pity that several transgressions have been forgotten, which many have trampled upon and treated as permitted, and are accustomed to commit communally on Shabbatot and the nights following Shabbatot and on festivals and appointed times, when groups upon groups, gatherings upon gatherings assemble to speak idle words, and “in a multitude of words transgression does not cease” — falsehood, mockery, slander, obscene speech, and the like — and there are those who gather to eat optional feasts. And there are places with a bad and bitter custom of gathering together once a week to play card games, making a party of it, increasing there laughter and levity, their session being a session of scoffers, and they drink and become drunk, and sing songs of frivolous flirtation, foreign songs, and waste the entire night in this, and one transgression drags along another transgression, for they lose the morning Shema and prayer, and spend much money to purchase for themselves a bad bargain in Gehinnom. Would that this bad and bitter custom be uprooted, and that there be no such thing in Israel, to commit such severe transgressions communally — let one who guards his soul distance himself from them. And happy are the Israelites, all of whom recite Psalms, but one who does these things — how is he not ashamed to recite (Psalms 1:1), “Happy is the man who has not walked,” etc., “and has not sat in the session of scoffers, but his desire is in the Torah of the Lord”? And let the God-fearing man not let these verses stray from before his eyes, and let him meditate in His Torah day and night.
Pele Yoetz 333:1: Regilut (Habituation) — All of Judaism depends on this, for only the beginnings are hard, and when a person accustoms himself to walk in good ways, the habit becomes second nature and it is no longer hard for him to do it — on the contrary, it becomes a delight to him, to the point that if once some incident or obstacle prevents him from doing that good thing he is habituated to, even if it is a matter of piety, it shall be hard for him, and it shall seem to him as though on that day he was not a Jew, and his flesh shall pain him and his soul shall mourn over him. And in this vein our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 63b): a person recites the Shema every day; if he does not recite it one day, it seems to him as though he never recited the Shema at all. Correspondingly, if a person commits a transgression and repeats it and becomes habituated to it, it becomes to him as though permitted (Kiddushin 20a), to the point that even if he hears from preachers among the common people, he will not abandon his bad habit. And it is a pity that several severe transgressions have become entirely treated as permitted by many of the common people because their habit is in an evil way, and even as they grow old they do not turn away from it — such as slander, vain oaths in foreign languages, taking the Name in vain, forbidden speech, forbidden sights, and many others, with neglect of Torah outweighing them all.
Pele Yoetz 333:2: And the man who is a Jew and believes what is said, that there is good reward for the righteous and evil and bitter punishment for the wicked, shall not destroy himself knowingly, but rather give his life to guard against every evil thing and fulfill every good thing, day by day, little by little establishing “turn from evil and do good” (Psalms 34:15). And if its beginning is painful, in time it shall become sweet and pleasant to him; his heart shall rejoice and his glory shall exult over drawing near to God, whom he approaches like one who finds abundant spoil.
Pele Yoetz 334:1: Rinah (Song) — It is known that the Torah is called “song,” as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Shemot Rabbah 47:5; Vayikra Rabbah 19:1): the song of Torah is only at night. And likewise one of the terms for prayer is “song” — there is a hint here, that one who reads Torah should read with pleasantness and joy, with a voice of song, and likewise prayer must be said with pleasantness and joy, with a voice of song, and especially the Song of the Sea and the recitation of Hallel, whose essence is to say them with a voice of song and thanksgiving, not in the manner of some places where the couriers rush through their recitation like the reading of the ten sons of Haman, and “enough to cause disgrace and wrath,” says the Name. Such song and Hallel — “offer it now to your governor” (Malachi 1:8) — will he accept you or show you favor? And likewise, saying the prayer and petitions and requests and blessings hastily is a great disgrace, even if a man were to speak this way to his fellow, and how much more so before a king of flesh and blood, who would certainly be angry at his voice, and he would be liable for his own life, for this is not the way one speaks when requesting and supplicating, and even to command his own servant in this manner, hastily, is a disgrace. And let a person visualize as though he were speaking in the vernacular in that same hasty manner, and he shall see and understand the disgracefulness of the matter and be ashamed and humiliated. And likewise reading the Torah hastily diminishes its value, and “who can discern errors?” And every reading has cantillation notes to sing the reading, and their secret is exalted and lofty, and whoever omits them loses much good.
Pele Yoetz 334:2: And reciting Mishnah with melody has no equal, and especially the Psalms, which are the remnants of King David, peace be upon him, and must be recited with a voice of song and thanksgiving. And how much shame comes to a person who says before reciting Psalms: “Just as we recite psalms in this world, so may we merit to say before You song and praise in the World to Come,” and afterward reads them hastily — woe to him if this is how he shall say song and praise in the World to Come; this is not song and praise but sorrow and sighing.
Pele Yoetz 334:3: And when reading communally and one person reads hastily, and likewise a prayer leader who is hasty in reciting the prayer, he bears the sin of the many, for against their will the couriers must go out in haste on his account, running after him and not catching up to him, so it turns out that they are coerced, and the one who rushes bears their sins upon his own soul and his own neck, and the Name has a grievance against these couriers, and especially many of the common people who, in reading hastily, stumble and fall, with an error in every word. Truly the Name might say: “Who has required this of you, to trample My courts?” (Isaiah 1:12) And why do you toil doubly toward Gehinnom, that you cause yourselves distress by giving up the pleasures of this world and force your inclination to stand in prayer and study, and yet when you read and pray hastily you stumble before Me? Would that his reward not be outweighed by his loss, and that the loss not exceed the praise, for this is like one who reviles and blasphemes, mentioning the holy Names while all the words are hurried and truncated. And though they said (Song of Songs 2:4), “And his banner over me was love,” [interpreted as] “and his skipping over me was love” (Shir HaShirim Rabbah), this applies only if, after effort and toil and reading with deliberation, he nonetheless, due to his foolishness, stammers in his speech — then he is considered before the Omnipresent like a small child who speaks with a stammering tongue and a halting speech, which is beloved and pleasant and delightful to those who hear it. But if a great man who can speak with good sense and understanding speaks with a halting tongue, this is like mockery and derision, and the listener shall rightly be angry, for he will say, “As one who mocks a man, have you toyed with me?” And would that they were wise and understood that a little with intention is better, and the Holy One, blessed be He, does not count pages but hours — it turns out that if you see a man swift in his work, the work of holiness, he should be called a fool and simpleton, for what does he need this trouble for? And our sages, of blessed memory, said (see Sanhedrin 101a): whoever reads a verse with proper melody brings redemption to the world.
Pele Yoetz 335:1: Refuah (Healing) — Our sages, of blessed memory, said, regarding the verse (Exodus 21:19), “And he shall surely heal him” — from here the Torah gave permission to the physician to heal (Berachot 60a). And they further said regarding the verse (Deuteronomy 28:59), “And sicknesses evil and enduring [ne'emanim]” — that they are faithful [ne'emanim] in their mission (Rashi there), for when they are sent, it is decreed upon them that they shall not depart except on a certain day, by the hand of a certain person, through a certain remedy (Yalkut Shimoni, Yitro, remez 289). And our sages, of blessed memory, further said (Sanhedrin 17b) that a person should not dwell in a place that has no physician.
Pele Yoetz 335:2: And behold, this inquiry has found a resting place: since the Name causes death and gives life, what does the physician give or add? Behold, if it were decreed that he die, even if all the physicians in the world were to stand by, they could not save his soul from death, and regarding this they said: “The physician's error is the Creator's will,” and none can save from His hand. And if it were decreed that he live without a physician, the Holy One, blessed be He, causes circumstances to turn and brings him his healing, for the Omnipresent has many methods and much redemption is with Him, and He shall send His word and heal them. But the answer to this and to many such inquiries is that there are three kinds of decrees: if it is a person who has merit standing by him, and his merit is strong and his fortune sound, even if he has no physician and does things contrary to his illness, he shall not die but shall surely live. And there is one upon whom death has been decreed, may the Merciful One save us, and even if he guards himself with every guard in the world, the guard watches in vain, and physicians will neither help nor save. But there is one whom, because of his sins, they leave under the workings of nature — if he guards himself and conducts himself with remedies according to nature, he shall surely live, and if not, he shall die, and regarding such a thing it is said (Proverbs 13:23), “And there is one swept away without justice.”
Pele Yoetz 335:3: Behold, therefore, every person must be concerned and must engage in remedies when necessary, for if he does not do so and is swept away without justice, he is liable for his own soul. And it is fitting to be liable for one's own soul, since he transgresses what is written in the Torah (Deuteronomy 4:15), “And you shall greatly guard your souls.” And the man who does not guard himself and does not conduct himself according to nature to seek a remedy for his illness when it is in his power to do so — besides that he shall be punished for transgressing what is written in the Torah, there is also this: that it turns out he relies on a miracle, and if a miracle is performed for him, they deduct from his merits (Shabbat 32[a]).
Pele Yoetz 335:4: And one must be exceedingly careful not to fall ill, and if he does fall ill, he must pursue remedies and expert physicians and not be sparing with money, for all that a man has he will give for his life. And they said in the holy Zohar that whoever deserves to be punished through his possessions falls into a sickbed and is not healed until he has spent the amount of possessions decreed against him. Behold, therefore, it is good to spend it quickly, and how good it is to increase charity, for it is a commandment in his hand, and its segulah is that it annuls the decree. And always, before engaging in remedies, let him believe with complete faith that his healing is in the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, a merciful and faithful Healer, who heals the sick of His people Israel, and let him precede with prayer before Him (and I, though poor, have already arranged a prayer for the sick and included it in my House of Prayers, with the help of Heaven).
Pele Yoetz 335:5: And whoever has a sick person in his house is obligated not to slumber, not to sleep, not to be still, and not to rest, until he has sought every kind of physician and every kind of remedy within his means. And if he is a poor man and lacks the means, the obligation falls upon the people of the city or upon the Bikur Cholim [visiting the sick] society to arrange physicians and remedies for him, and they should not be concerned about the great expense, for it shall be counted as a great commandment. Go and learn how far the obligation of healing extends, for they permitted desecrating the severe Shabbat and transgressing the entire Torah for the sake of healing a sick person in danger, because they said (Shabbat 151b): better to desecrate one Shabbat so that he may keep many Shabbatot. And how much more so and how much more certainly is it fitting to spend all the money in the world in order to preserve one soul of Israel, which is as though he preserved an entire world. And if, despite all this, the sick person dies, Heaven forbid, this shall not be a stumbling block or an occasion of sin for them, and their hearts shall rejoice that they did what was incumbent upon them to do. And the Name does what is good in His eyes, and He shall repay them sevenfold into their bosom, wealth and riches in their house.
Pele Yoetz 336:1: Rofeh (Physician) — The physician must inquire and search with wisdom before engaging in medicine, so that he not go out of line and, in place of a remedy, cause harm. And how greatly must he watch with seven eyes lest he err in his own imagination, for he handles a soul, and the Holy One, blessed be He, shall demand his blood from his own hand. And he should not engage in the craft of medicine to heal Israel unless he is exceedingly, exceedingly expert in the wisdom of medicine.
Pele Yoetz 336:2: And there are now many common people, especially in the cities of Ishmael, quack physicians who take up the craft of medicine as an occupation to earn a livelihood, and they have never seen light nor ever studied the wisdom of medicine — only the man whose spirit moved him to approach this craft acquires for himself the name of an expert physician, and he engages in the craft of medicine as a blind man gropes in the darkness, not knowing his right hand from his left. Woe to such physicians, of whom it was said (Kiddushin 82a), “The best of physicians is destined for Gehinnom,” for they cause much bloodshed in the world. And not everyone who wishes to take the name “expert physician” may come and take it (Berachot 47b), but only if he himself knows he is expert in the wisdom of medicine. And even if he is expert, if he encounters an illness he does not recognize, he should not be ashamed to say, “This is not my area; go to an expert,” for he must not toy with this person's blood. And in a place where there are no other men available, one should strive to become such an expert, as is the custom in places without a physician, where each person teaches one remedy, one saying this and another saying that — in any case, they must be careful not to learn or perform a remedy not on the authority of an expert, unless it is something clear to them that if it does not help, it will not harm.
Pele Yoetz 336:3: And every physician should precede trouble with prayer, and go to a sage who will teach him, so that his prayer be fluent in his mouth to recite; every day let him pour out his soul before the Name, that He be among his helpers so that he not err and no mishap result from his hand, and that healing come through him — perhaps there is hope. And the physician must run like a deer as soon as he is called to a sick person, even at midnight, whether for the rich or the poor alike. And let him go to visit the sick person every day, and if necessary, several times a day, for the sick person's eyes are fixed upon the physician, and every time the physician enters to see him, he revives his soul, and it shall be counted as a great commandment for him. And it is fitting to treat the poor for free just as he treats the wealthy for payment, and his reward shall be doubled and redoubled from Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 336:4: And it is fitting for the physician and for all who visit the sick person to show the sick person a cheerful face and strengthen him with words so that he not fear and not be dismayed, that no evil befall him, with the help of Heaven; but let him tell him that in any case it is good and beneficial for healing to pray to the Name and contemplate thoughts of repentance, and to pour out speech to seek forgiveness from the Master of masters, for He is the true Healer — when a man's ways please Him, He shall send His word and heal him. Regarding one who does these things it is said (Psalms 41:2), “Happy is he who considers the poor” [i.e., the sick person] — “in the day of evil the Lord shall deliver him; the Lord shall guard him and revive him,” etc.
Pele Yoetz 337:1: Rechitzah (Washing) — Washing the face every day is a commandment: “Prepare to meet your God, O Israel” (Amos 4:12). And it is out of respect for God, to honor His image, for God made man in His image (Genesis 9:6), as they said in the Talmud. But one must be careful to first dry the hands, to remove the evil spirit that rests upon them. And the obligation is even greater to wash one's face, hands, and feet in warm water on Friday, and it must be done specifically in this order: first the face, then the hands, then the feet. And how good it is if one can wash his entire body at the bathhouse and also immerse in a mikveh of purity, and let him know that there are supernal secrets in all this, and he is assured of meriting an additional soul, spirit, and higher soul that come with Shabbat. And the man who is hasty for wealth lacks this too, for he does not come home until close to darkness. But the man who is pure should close his shop close to Minchah time and receive Shabbat with joy according to the law and halachah, and there the Lord shall command the blessing (Deuteronomy 28:8).
Pele Yoetz 337:2: And it is known that on the Ninth of Av and Yom Kippur, washing is forbidden, like eating and drinking, for the entire day until nightfall, and even for the morning hand-washing or upon leaving the privy, they permitted washing only up to the joints of the fingers (Orach Chaim, sec. 554, para. 10), and simple folk have transgressed and wash their faces and hands as on any other day — may the Good Name grant atonement for it. And because of this, an obligation rests upon everyone who knows the law to warn and remind, so that they not stretch out their unclean hands, but rather do what is incumbent upon them.
Pele Yoetz 338:1: Rabbo (One's Teacher) — Great is the obligation to honor and revere one's teacher, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 108a; Avot 4:12): let the fear of your teacher be like the fear of Heaven. And they said (Shabbat 30b; Pesachim 117a): any student who sits before his teacher and whose lips do not drip myrrh [i.e., proper deference] — the sign of dread and fear should be upon him. And it is forbidden to render a halachic ruling in the presence of one's teacher, for they said (Berachot 31b): whoever renders a halachic ruling in the presence of his teacher is liable to death. And even a matter as simple as an egg in broth, he may not rule on. And who is greater to us than Nadav and Avihu and Joshua bin Nun, who transgressed this and were punished? And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 110a): whoever disputes his teacher is as one who disputes the Divine Presence. And there are many other such statements of our sages, of blessed memory. And behold, while they are young and sit before their teacher, certainly the fear of their teacher is upon them, for he might strike them with a rod on their head; but it is even more necessary to urge caution when they grow up and become wise in their own eyes — there are unreliable sons who treat their teacher's honor lightly, to the point that their teacher would say of them (Isaiah 1:2), “Sons I have raised and exalted, but they have rebelled against Me.”
Pele Yoetz 338:2: And it is all the more necessary to urge caution for one whose father is a sage and is also his teacher, for his obligation is doubled and redoubled, and because of his great familiarity with him he becomes overly familiar with his father, and through this he sins against his father. And though we have established (Kiddushin 32b) that a teacher who forgoes his own honor, his honor is forgone, and certainly this is the trait of every good person, to forgo his own honor so that no one be punished on his account — how much more so a teacher toward his student, whose honor should be as dear to him as his own, and how much more so a father toward his sons, who are bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, and he does not want them punished on his account — but in any case, if they are not careful, they lack a great commandment and lose much good, and especially since they said that although his honor is forgone, disgracing him is not forgone. And whoever treats honor lightly will not refrain from doing things that are a disgrace and grief to them, and he shall certainly be punished, Heaven forbid. Therefore let them fear for their own souls lest they be burned by their coals, and let them gather strength and exert effort to be careful about the honor of their father and mother and the honor of their teacher, and through this they shall merit the crown of Torah, and let them be careful not to cause grief and anger to their father, mother, and teacher, for this causes grief and anger to our Father in Heaven, and one who gives them satisfaction gives satisfaction to his Creator, and He shall cause his lamp to shine and his crown to blossom upon him.
Pele Yoetz 339:1: Ratzon (Contentment) — Whoever is full of contentment shall not be resentful nor angry about anything, and shall not be distressed nor grieved about anything in the world. There is no better trait than this — joy for the body and rest for the soul, and this is a gift of God. And in any case, even one whose nature is bad can reverse and change it through deepening and persisting in pure thoughts, and through strengthening himself to remove anger and grief from his heart and to remove evil from his flesh by the power of true arguments that indeed exist, not to follow vanity, for whoever suffers this suffers that too [i.e., troubles are relative], and understanding is easy for the discerning. And if a man gives his mind to settle with correct and composed understanding, to seek the truth and distance himself from all bad and forbidden traits, as soon as he opens his eyes a little, with his own eyes he shall see the disgracefulness of bad traits, which are vanity and vexation of spirit, and truth stands while falsehood has no legs to stand on. But this is the evil of man on earth: that he strengthens himself in his own thinking and draws himself to seek arguments and give falsehood legs to stand on, until in the end it seems to him that truth is with him and his way is upright in his own eyes, and he reinforces it with nails so it will not be moved, and he goes from evil to evil, and his flesh pains him and his soul mourns over him, that in the end he inherits Gehinnom, may the Merciful One save us (and see what I have written above under the entry Middot and under the entry Iyun).
